prompt: What is a polypropylene called in which all the methyl groups are on the same side of the zigzag backbone?

choices.text: Isotactic
Syndiotactic
choices.why: In syndiotactic polypropylene the methyl groups alternate regularly on opposite sides of the backbone.

choices.text: Atactic
choices.why: In atactic polypropylene the methyl groups are oriented randomly.

choices.text: Racemic
choices.why: Racemic describes a mixture of enantiomers, not the arrangement of methyl groups along a chain. All on one side is isotactic.

explanation: A polymer with all methyl groups on the same side of the zigzag backbone is isotactic; one in which the methyl groups alternate regularly on opposite sides is syndiotactic; and one with its methyl groups randomly oriented is atactic (Figure 31.2.1).

prompt: A polypropylene chain has its methyl groups alternating regularly on opposite sides of the zigzag backbone. What is this form called?

choices.text: Syndiotactic
Isotactic
choices.why: Isotactic polypropylene has all its methyl groups on the same side of the backbone.

choices.text: Atactic
choices.why: Atactic polypropylene has randomly oriented methyl groups. A regular alternation is syndiotactic.

choices.text: Alternating
choices.why: Alternating describes a copolymer in which two different monomer units alternate (Section 31.3). The stereochemical term is syndiotactic.

explanation: Syndiotactic polypropylene has its methyl groups alternating regularly on opposite sides of the backbone. Isotactic has them all on the same side, and atactic has them randomly oriented.

prompt: How do the three stereochemical forms of polypropylene compare in how they can be made?

choices.text: Radical initiators don't work well, but Ziegler–Natta catalysts can give isotactic, syndiotactic, or atactic polypropylene
Radical initiators give the isotactic form, and Ziegler–Natta catalysts give only the atactic form
choices.why: Propylene polymerization with radical initiators does not work well. Ziegler–Natta catalysts can give all three forms.

choices.text: Only the atactic form can be made, because the chirality centers form at random
choices.why: With the right Ziegler–Natta catalyst system, isotactic and syndiotactic forms can be made as well as atactic.

choices.text: All three forms have identical properties, so the catalyst doesn't matter
choices.why: The three forms have somewhat different properties, and the catalyst system decides which one forms.

explanation: The three forms of polypropylene all have somewhat different properties, and all can be made by using the right catalyst. Propylene polymerization using radical initiators does not work well, but Ziegler–Natta catalysts allow preparation of isotactic, syndiotactic, and atactic polypropylene.

prompt: Which combination of reagents is a typical preparation of a Ziegler–Natta catalyst?

choices.text: Triethylaluminum, (CH3CH2)3Al, with titanium tetrachloride, TiCl4
BF3 with a small amount of water
choices.why: That gives the acid catalyst used for cationic polymerization of isobutylene (Section 31.1).

choices.text: Butyllithium with styrene
choices.why: Butyllithium is an anionic initiator for styrene (Section 31.1), not a Ziegler–Natta catalyst.

choices.text: Benzoyl peroxide with heat
choices.why: Benzoyl peroxide is a radical initiator. Ziegler–Natta catalysts are made from an alkylaluminum and a titanium compound.

explanation: Ziegler–Natta catalysts, of which there are many formulations, are organometallic transition-metal complexes made by treating an alkylaluminum with a titanium compound. Triethylaluminum with titanium tetrachloride is a typical preparation.

prompt: Ziegler–Natta catalysts revolutionized polymer chemistry after 1953 because of two advantages. What are they?

choices.text: The polymers are linear with practically no branching, and their stereochemistry can be controlled
The polymers are highly branched, and they always form the atactic form
choices.why: Ziegler–Natta polymers are linear, with practically no chain branching, and isotactic, syndiotactic, or atactic forms can be chosen.

choices.text: They work with any vinyl monomer, and no metal is needed
choices.why: Ziegler–Natta catalysts are titanium–aluminum complexes. Working with practically any vinyl monomer is the advantage of radical polymerization.

choices.text: They give copolymers only, and the chains are heavily cross-linked
choices.why: Neither is true. The two advantages are linear chains and stereochemical control.

explanation: Following their introduction in 1953, Ziegler–Natta catalysts revolutionized polymer chemistry because, first, the resultant polymers are linear, with practically no chain branching, and second, they are stereochemically controllable: isotactic, syndiotactic, and atactic forms can all be produced, depending on the catalyst system used.

prompt: How does a Ziegler–Natta catalyst add an alkene monomer to the growing chain?

choices.text: The alkene coordinates to a vacant site on titanium and then inserts into the carbon–titanium bond
A radical on titanium adds to the alkene, giving a carbon radical that adds to the next monomer
choices.why: The active catalyst is an alkyltitanium intermediate with a vacant coordination site, not a radical.

choices.text: The titanium protonates the alkene to give a carbocation
choices.why: That would be cationic polymerization. In the Ziegler–Natta process the coordinated alkene inserts into the carbon–titanium bond.

choices.text: The alkene forms a four-membered ring with titanium that opens to exchange substituents
choices.why: That describes the metallacycle in olefin metathesis (Section 31.5). The Ziegler–Natta step is coordination followed by insertion.

explanation: The active form of a Ziegler–Natta catalyst is an alkyltitanium intermediate with a vacant coordination site on the metal. The alkene coordinates to the titanium and then inserts into the carbon–titanium bond to extend the alkyl chain. A new coordination site opens up during insertion, so the process repeats.

prompt: How does high-density polyethylene (HDPE) from the Ziegler–Natta process differ from low-density polyethylene (LDPE)?

choices.text: HDPE is linear and highly crystalline with greater strength and heat resistance; LDPE is the branched product of radical polymerization
HDPE is the branched product of radical polymerization; LDPE is linear and made by Ziegler–Natta catalysts
choices.why: This reverses the two. The Ziegler–Natta process gives linear HDPE; radical-induced polymerization gives branched LDPE.

choices.text: HDPE has fewer than 1000 ethylene units per chain, while LDPE has 4000 to 7000
choices.why: HDPE has 4000 to 7000 ethylene units per chain, with molecular weights of 100,000 to 200,000 amu.

choices.text: HDPE is weaker and less heat resistant, so it is used only for thin films
choices.why: HDPE has greater strength and heat resistance than LDPE and is used for plastic squeeze bottles and molded housewares.

explanation: The linear polyethylene from the Ziegler–Natta process, high-density polyethylene, is highly crystalline, with 4000 to 7000 ethylene units per chain and molecular weights of 100,000 to 200,000 amu. It has greater strength and heat resistance than branched low-density polyethylene from radical-induced polymerization, and is used for squeeze bottles and molded housewares.

prompt: Ultrahigh-molecular-weight (UHMW) polyethylene contains more than how many monomer units per chain?
explanation: UHMW polyethylene contains more than 100,000 monomer units per chain and has molecular weights from 3,000,000 to 6,000,000 amu. By comparison, HMW polyethylene has 10,000 to 18,000 units and HDPE 4000 to 7000.

prompt: Vinylidene chloride, H2C=CCl2, does not polymerize in isotactic, syndiotactic, and atactic forms. Why not?

choices.text: Its polymer, made of –CH2–CCl2– units, has no chirality centers
It cannot be polymerized at all
choices.why: Vinylidene chloride does polymerize; it is a monomer of Saran (Section 31.3). Its polymer simply has no chirality centers.

choices.text: Its polymer is always racemic
choices.why: Being racemic is about optical rotation. The reason here is that no backbone carbon of –CH2–CCl2– carries four different groups.

choices.text: Ziegler–Natta catalysts don't react with chlorine-containing alkenes
choices.why: The section's answer is structural: each CCl2 carbon has two identical chlorines, so the polymer has no chirality centers.

explanation: Tacticity describes the relative orientation of substituents at the chirality centers along a chain. In poly(vinylidene chloride), every backbone carbon is either CH2 or CCl2, so none has four different groups. The polymer has no chirality centers (Exercise 31.2.1), so isotactic, syndiotactic, and atactic forms don't exist.

prompt: Polypropylene chains contain many chirality centers. Would a sample of isotactic, syndiotactic, or atactic polypropylene rotate plane-polarized light?

choices.text: No; the samples are racemic and have no optical rotation
Yes; only the isotactic form rotates light, because all its methyl groups are on one side
choices.why: The answer to Exercise 31.2.2 says the polymers are racemic, so no form shows optical rotation.

choices.text: Yes; all three forms rotate light, because every chain has many chirality centers
choices.why: Having chirality centers isn't enough. The samples are racemic, so their rotations cancel.

choices.text: Only the atactic form rotates light, because its methyl groups are random
choices.why: None of the three forms rotates light; the polymers are racemic.

explanation: Although polypropylene has many chirality centers, samples of isotactic, syndiotactic, and atactic polypropylene are racemic and show no optical rotation (Exercise 31.2.2).
